rows.selection_reason: With no prior experiments, the highest-priority question is establishing a strong multimodal singleprofile baseline to anchor all subsequent comparisons. config_009 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l, concat fusion, singleprofile) is chosen because: (1) it pairs a learned RNA embedding (scvi_n200) with a strong pretrained image encoder (ViT-L), representing a well-motivated 'default strong' multimodal setup; (2) concat fusion is the simplest fusion strategy, avoiding confounding from learned weighting; (3) singleprofile keeps the experiment focused on the core question of whether the two modalities, when simply combined, provide a useful signal. This baseline will serve as the reference point for all follow-up experiments testing whether removing a modality (image_only/rna_only), changing the RNA encoder, switching to multiprofile+aggregation, or altering fusion actually improves or degrades performance. Under a limited budget, anchoring the search around a clear, interpretable multimodal reference is more informative than starting with a unimodal baseline (which would leave the multimodal ceiling unknown) or a complex multiprofile configuration (which would conflate multiple design choices).

With only one completed experiment (config_009: multimodal, scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l, singleprofile, concat fusion, acc≈0.53), the most critical uncertainty is whether the multimodal fusion is actually adding value over a single-modality baseline. config_002 (image_only, singleprofile, imagenet_vit_l) is the cleanest controlled comparison: it removes the RNA modality while keeping the identical image encoder, profile setting, and overall architecture, isolating the contribution of RNA and the fusion mechanism. If image-only approaches or exceeds 0.53, the multimodal premise is questionable and budget should shift toward single-modality optimization; if it is substantially lower, it validates the multimodal direction and justifies further investment in fusion/aggregation/profile design. This single experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about the foundational design decision (is multimodal worth the complexity?) before committing budget to finer-grained comparisons like encoder choice, aggregation, or multiprofile settings.

We have two data points: multimodal (scvi_n200 + ViT-L, concat) at 0.532 acc and image-only (ViT-L) at 0.227 acc. The critical missing piece is the RNA-only baseline with the same scvi_n200 encoder and singleprofile setting. Config_003 (rna_only, singleprofile, scvi_n200) completes the modality ablation: if RNA-only approaches 0.532, the image modality adds little and future effort should focus on RNA representation; if it is substantially lower, fusion is genuinely beneficial and we should invest in better fusion/aggregation. This single experiment resolves the most important uncertainty—whether the multimodal gain is driven by RNA alone or by true cross-modal synergy—before spending budget on more complex multiprofile or fusion variants.

Evidence: config_009 (multimodal, scvi_n200, vit_l, concat) achieves 0.532 acc, only ~1.2% above RNA-only (config_003, 0.520), while image-only (config_002) is very weak at 0.227. This suggests the image modality contributes a small signal that may be underutilized by the current concat fusion. Question: config_024 is identical to config_009 except fusion changes from concat to weighted, providing a clean single-variable A/B test of whether the fusion strategy can amplify the image contribution. Why this is the best next experiment: it isolates the fusion effect without confounding changes to encoder, profile setting, or aggregation. If weighted fusion meaningfully improves accuracy, it reveals that fusion design is a lever worth further exploration (and justifies testing other fusion variants). If it does not, it strengthens the hypothesis that the image signal is inherently limited under singleprofile, redirecting effort toward multiprofile or alternative encoders. Under a limited budget, this minimal-change comparison maximizes information per experiment about a key design decision.

All four completed experiments use singleprofile; the multiprofile dimension (and its associated aggregation choice) is entirely unexplored, representing the largest source of uncertainty. The best-performing config so far is config_024 (multimodal, singleprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, weighted; acc 0.5375). config_017 is the most direct extension of that configuration: it changes only the profile setting to multiprofile and adds avgpool aggregation, while keeping the same RNA encoder, image encoder, and weighted fusion. This isolates the effect of multiprofile + simple aggregation. If it improves over 0.5375, multiprofile is a promising direction to further explore (e.g., transformer aggregation); if it degrades, we learn that the single-profile scvi representation is already sufficient and can redirect budget toward RNA encoder or image encoder variants. Under a limited budget, testing the simplest multiprofile variant first is more informative than jumping to a complex transformer aggregation, because it establishes a clean baseline for the aggregation axis.

Evidence: config_017 (multiprofile, avgpool, weighted) achieved 0.706 acc, a dramatic jump over all singleprofile configs (~0.53). The key untested question is whether avgpool is specifically important or whether a more expressive aggregation (transformer) could further improve performance. config_025 is a clean single-variable comparison to config_017, changing only aggregation from avgpool to transformer while holding scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, multiprofile, and weighted fusion constant. This is the best next experiment because: (1) it isolates the aggregation mechanism that appears to drive the largest performance gain observed so far, (2) the prior singleprofile data (config_009 vs config_024) showed fusion method has only marginal effect (~0.005), suggesting aggregation is the more impactful design axis to probe, and (3) the result generalizes—if transformer outperforms avgpool here, it likely does so across other encoder combinations, guiding all subsequent multiprofile experiments efficiently under the limited budget.

Evidence: The jump from singleprofile (~0.53) to multiprofile+transformer+weighted (0.725, config_025) is dramatic, but we cannot yet attribute this improvement to the image modality versus the multiprofile RNA representation alone. RNA singleprofile alone achieved 0.520, and multimodal singleprofile only reached 0.532, suggesting the image contributes very little in singleprofile mode. Question: config_013 (rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, transformer) isolates whether the multiprofile+transformer RNA pipeline alone can approach 0.725, or whether the image encoder (imagenet_vit_l) is providing a meaningful complementary signal in the multiprofile setting. Why this is the best next experiment: It changes only one factor (removing the image) from the current best configuration, cleanly separating the contribution of the image modality from the profile/aggregation gains. If rna_only multiprofile+transformer approaches 0.72, the image is unnecessary and we should focus budget on RNA encoder and profile choices; if it falls well short, the multimodal fusion is justified and we should exploit that direction. This single experiment resolves the most fundamental design uncertainty before spending further budget on encoder or fusion variations.

The strongest evidence so far shows that multiprofile + transformer aggregation + weighted fusion with scvi_n200 and imagenet_vit_l achieves the best performance (config_025: 0.725 acc / 0.685 F1), and that multiprofile is the dominant design lever (~0.18 gain over singleprofile). However, the RNA encoder choice is the largest untested dimension—we have only ever used scvi_n200. Config_019 is a clean single-variable swap (scvi_n200 → pca_n2000) within the best-performing multiprofile/transformer/weighted/imagenet_vit_l setup. This directly tests whether a learned RNA representation (scvi) adds meaningful value over a simple linear one (PCA-2000) in the regime where the model is already strong. If pca_n2000 matches scvi_n200, it tells us the RNA encoder is not a bottleneck and we can redirect budget toward image encoder or fusion; if it degrades substantially, it confirms the learned encoder's importance and justifies further investment in scgpt or other learned encoders. This is the highest-information-per-experiment choice because it isolates one critical, completely unexplored variable in the most promising configuration.

Evidence: The multiprofile + transformer + weighted fusion + imagenet_vit_l pipeline is clearly the strongest architecture (config_025: 0.725 acc vs 0.537 for single-profile). Within that pipeline, scvi_n200 substantially outperforms pca_n2000 (0.725 vs 0.586), showing the RNA encoder is a critical design axis. However, scgpt has never been tested, leaving a major uncertainty about whether it could surpass scvi_n200 or underperform like pca_n2000. Question: config_011 (scgpt, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted, multiprofile) is identical to the best-performing config_025 except for the RNA encoder, cleanly isolating the encoder effect. Why best next experiment: The RNA encoder is the most consequential unexplored variable—two of three encoders have been tested and showed a ~0.14 acc gap, so the third could shift the ranking meaningfully. Resolving this now prevents wasting future budget on suboptimal encoders in downstream combinations (e.g., with resnet50 or different fusion). It is a single-variable change from the current best, maximizing information per experiment.

The current best configuration (config_025: scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted, multiprofile; acc=0.725) has been validated across RNA encoder (scvi_n200 >> pca_n2000 > scgpt) and aggregation (transformer > avgpool) choices. However, the image encoder effect has never been isolated in the multiprofile setting—all completed multiprofile experiments use imagenet_vit_l. Config_034 changes only the image encoder to resnet50 while keeping scvi_n200, transformer, weighted, and multiprofile fixed, providing a clean single-variable comparison against config_025. This is the highest-value next experiment because: (1) it resolves the largest remaining uncertainty about a core design axis, (2) if resnet50 is competitive it broadens the feasible design space, and (3) if it underperforms significantly it confirms imagenet_vit_l as a necessary component, preventing wasted budget on resnet50-based variants. No other single experiment reduces as much uncertainty about the optimal architecture under the limited budget.
